q: The technician hands you the inventory list and you count the galley gear together. What do you do before you sign?
a: Have him write 'forks 6, pans 2' on the list and sign that
o: Sign it — two forks and a pan are not worth the time
Sign it and buy the missing ones in town for the base
Sign it and count again properly on the first evening
why: What is written as missing at check-in cannot be charged as lost at check-out.

fig.title: Inventory list — galley
lines: You count: forks 6, pans 2, the rest OK

q: Three items on the deck inventory are not aboard. The technician says they are in the store and will be brought before you leave. What do you do?
a: Note all three as missing on the list now; strike them out when they arrive
o: Sign the list as it is — he said he will bring them before you leave
Sign the list and remind him again on Monday by phone from the first bay
Refuse to take the boat until the store has delivered all three
why: The list you sign is the check-out baseline; a promised item that never comes is charged at list price.

fig.title: Deck inventory
lines: Technician: 'in the store, I'll bring them'

q: You look into the cabins while the technician is on deck. What do you do?
a: Ask for the mattress dried or changed and the latch fixed, and note both on the form
o: Air the mattress at sea and tape the door; neither is deposit material
Note the latch only — a damp mattress is normal on a boat
Say nothing now and raise both at check-out so they are not charged
why: Faults you accept silently become yours at check-out; the base can still fix them on Saturday.

fig.title: Cabins
lines: Stbd aft: door latch broken, door swings

q: The technician points at the galley and says everything in it works. What do you do?
a: Switch the fridge on, light every burner and the oven, boil the kettle before he leaves
o: Take his word for it — galley gear is not part of the deposit anyway
Light one burner; the fridge needs hours to get cold anyway
Test it all on the first evening and call the base if anything fails
why: Test what you are told works while the technician is aboard; a failure at sea is yours to live with.

q: On Wednesday you touch the quay at Fiskardo and chip the gelcoat at the bow. What do you do?
a: Photograph it and phone the base the same day; the repair comes off the deposit at check-out
o: Say nothing — a chip that size is either found at check-out or it is not
Touch it up with a repair kit from the chandler so that it is not found
Wait and point it out yourself at the check-out, which is honest enough
why: Reporting at once keeps the insurance and the waiver valid; hidden or late damage can cost the whole deposit.

fig.title: Wednesday, Fiskardo quay
lines: Gelcoat chip at the bow, 3 cm
Contract: any damage reported at once

q: Thursday evening you are in an anchorage 30 miles from the base and see this forecast. What do you do?
a: Call the base now, say where you are, and decide with their advice: move tonight or sit it out
o: Leave Friday morning regardless — the penalty is worse than a rough passage
Stay put and call the base on Saturday morning once it has eased
Slip at 04:00 without telling anyone and hope to beat the wind
why: The decision is the skipper's, but a base warned the day before can plan; a penalty is never a reason to sail into a gale.

fig.title: Thursday 18:00
lines: Forecast Fri: NW 7, gusts 8, easing Sat noon
Contract: back at base Fri by 18:00
Late return: €500 a day + next crew's costs

q: Friday afternoon you are approaching the base. The briefing said return berths are assigned on arrival. What do you do?
a: Call the base on the VHF or phone before entering and take the berth they give you
o: Take the first empty berth on the base pontoon — their boats all come back tonight
Anchor off at C tonight and come in at 08:00 for the check-out
Go alongside the fuel dock at A and wait there for a marinero
why: The return berth, the time and the mooring are the base's; 'back at the base' means alongside, before the deadline.

fig.note: Friday 16:30 · contract: alongside at the base by 18:00

q: Friday 15:30, the fuel gauge shows half. The base has given you berth B for the night. Where do you go first?
a: Fuel dock A: fill the tank and keep the receipt, then berth B
o: Berth B — the base refuels every boat and takes it from the deposit
Berth B now, fuel dock A at 08:00 before the technician comes
Berth B — half a tank is enough for the base's next crew
why: 'Returned full' is in the contract; the base's own refuelling adds a service charge, and the receipt is your proof.

fig.note: Contract: full tank, or pump price + €50 service

q: You are three miles from the base on Friday afternoon with these tanks. What do you do before the check-out?
a: Pump the holding tank out where allowed offshore or at the base, and fill the water at the berth
o: Leave both as they are — filling water and pumping out are part of the final cleaning
Pump the holding tank out in the base marina after dark, when nobody is watching
Fill the water from jerry cans and leave the holding tank for the next crew to empty
why: Water full and holding tank empty are check-out items; discharge only offshore where the local rules allow, or at a pump-out.

fig.title: Check-out form — tanks
lines: Contract: water full, holding tank empty
Your water: ¼ · holding tank: ½
Gas: in use ⅓, spare full — write it down

q: It is Friday evening at the base and the crew asks how much cleaning the boat needs. What do you tell them?
a: Clean the galley, fridge and heads and take the rubbish ashore; the base does the rest
o: Scrub the whole boat inside and out — cleaning is the charterer's job
Leave it all — the final cleaning is paid for in the price
Pay the €80 — it is cheaper than the crew's last evening
why: Read the clause: the included cleaning covers the boat, not your rubbish or a dirty fridge and heads.

fig.title: Contract — cleaning
lines: Final cleaning: included in the price
Galley, fridge and heads left clean

q: You are back at the base on Friday with the dinghy still in the water and the outboard on it. What do you do before the check-out?
a: Rinse both with fresh water and lift them back to where they were at check-in
o: Leave both in the water at the berth — the base lifts them with the crane
Deflate the dinghy and stow it with the outboard in the aft locker
Tie them off astern and tell the technician at check-out where they are
why: The dinghy and outboard go back washed, lifted and stowed as at check-in; they are inventory, checked like the rest.

q: Saturday 07:30, the technician is due at eight. The crew is still in their bunks and the saloon is full of bags. What do you do?
a: Get the crew up, bags into the cockpit, cabins stripped and clear by eight
o: Let them sleep — the check-out is the skipper's business
Ask the technician to come back at eleven when the boat is empty
Pack after the inspection — the boat is yours until the next crew boards
why: The inspection needs empty cabins and lockers; the base turns the boat round the same day.

fig.title: Contract — handover
lines: Boat back at base: Friday by 18:00

q: At the check-out the technician fills in the engine hours on the form. What do you do?
a: Read the meter with him and have the form corrected to 1 412 before you sign
o: Let it go — nine hours matter only to the base's service schedule
Write 1 371 plus the hours you logged each day instead of the meter
Sign it — the figure is the base's, not yours, and the fuel is full
why: Both readings are compared on the form you sign; a wrong figure is argued later only with your photo.

q: The technician's walk-round finds nothing new. Then the diver comes up. What do you do?
a: Ask for the diver's photo and compare it with your check-in photos of the keel before agreeing
o: Accept the €350 — at every base the diver's word on the hull is final
Refuse outright — the check-in form already says the keel has scratches
Sign now and dispute the €350 by e-mail with the base once you are home
why: New damage is settled against the check-in form and photos; 'old scratches' on the form only covers what the photos show.

fig.title: Check-out inspection
lines: Diver: scratch on the keel, 20 cm, 'fresh'

q: At the check-out the technician marks a scratch on the starboard quarter as new. What do you do?
a: Show the dated check-in photo and ask for the charge to be withdrawn and the form amended now
o: Pay the €200 — you signed 'hull OK' and the form you signed is the contract
Offer to split it — the form is against you but the photo is for you
Pay now and claim it back from your deposit insurance when you are home
why: A dated check-in photo is the evidence the base itself asked you to take; a charge is disputed at the base, before signing.

fig.title: Check-out — hull
lines: Your photo, Sat 15:42: the same scratch

q: The cockpit table came off its hinge on Thursday. At the check-out the base wants a new table. What do you do?
a: Point to the check-in note: a fault recorded as old is wear, not new damage, and not yours
o: Pay — it broke on your watch and the deposit covers wear and tear
Pay half — the hinge was old but the break happened to you
Refuse to sign anything and leave the base with the deposit still held
why: The check-in form is the baseline: what was noted as old or defective at check-in cannot be charged as new damage.

fig.title: Check-out — cockpit table
lines: Base: new table €420 from the deposit
You reported it on Thursday by phone

q: A winch handle and a fender went overboard during the week. What do you expect at the check-out?
a: A €150 deduction at the base's list prices, shown on the settlement
o: No deduction — the deposit covers damage, not lost gear
A deduction at the chandler's retail price plus the base's time
A claim on the deposit insurance, which pays for losses too
why: Lost inventory is charged from the deposit at the base's list price; deposit insurance normally excludes it.

q: The technician shows you this settlement and asks you to sign. What do you ask for first?
a: An itemised receipt with the repair estimate, and the date the card hold is released
o: The €2,590 in cash — a hold on the card can take weeks to come back
Only the keel estimate — the fender is a fixed price from the list
Nothing more — the settlement is written out and signed by the base
why: Every deduction comes with a receipt and the repair cost; the pre-authorisation is released by the base, not by your bank on its own.

fig.title: Deposit settlement
lines: Release of the rest: 'in a few days'

q: During the week you noted the autopilot dropping out above 20 knots, a stiff heads pump and a flickering port light. Nobody is charging you for any of it. What do you do at the check-out?
a: Give the technician a short written list for the base's job sheet
o: Keep it to yourself — anything you report may end as a deduction
Post it in an online review so the next crew is warned
Mention the port light only — the rest is normal charter wear
why: A fault list costs you nothing, gets fixed before the next crew and shows the base you sailed with care.

q: Saturday morning you lock the boat. A crew mate says to switch everything off, as on his own boat. What do you do?
a: Follow the base's note: shore power on, house on, engine off, hatches shut, keys to the office
o: Switch everything off and unplug the shore cable, as on his boat
Leave everything on, instruments too, so the base sees they work
Switch everything off and leave the key in the ignition for the technician
why: The base's note is what the next check-in depends on: the charger keeps the batteries up and the fridge cold.

fig.title: Base note — leaving the boat
lines: Battery switches: house ON, engine OFF
Hatches and ports closed, bimini folded
